---
name: project-tracker
description: Manage a generic work-tracking system — create tasks, schedule across calendars, and roll up reports. Use when the user asks to add a task, find a meeting slot, or summarize project activity. Routes to the correct sub-skill.
---

# project-tracker

A single entry point over a work-tracking system with three **unrelated**
capabilities. Each capability lives in its own sub-skill because the steps,
templates, and reference material share nothing with the others.

## What this skill does

Pick the sub-skill that matches the task at hand. Do not read the others —
they will only waste context.

| If the user wants to… | Load sub-skill |
| --- | --- |
| add / create a task | `sub-skills/task-creation/` |
| find a time to meet / schedule | `sub-skills/calendar-scheduling/` |
| summarize / report / roll up activity | `sub-skills/reporting/` |

## Layout

- `reference/` — shared reference material (API limits, field mapping, property glossary).
- `scripts/` — shared scripts: `shared-auth.sh` loads a session token before
  any API call, `new-ticket.sh` scaffolds a task body, `status-report.sh`
  prints a status digest.
- `sub-skills/` — one directory per independent capability.

Each sub-skill has its own `SKILL.md` plus its own templates, scripts, or
queries. Start there; the root `SKILL.md` should stay small.

---
name: project-tracker-calendar-scheduling
description: Find an open meeting slot across calendars. Use when the user wants to schedule, find a time, or book a meeting. Reads availability and suggests slots; does not create tasks.
---

# Calendar scheduling

Find a free time window across one or more calendars. This is unrelated to
task creation and reporting — it reads availability only and suggests slots.

## Steps

1. Source the shared token: `bash scripts/shared-auth.sh`.
2. Collect the calendars and the desired duration.
3. Run `scripts/find-slots.sh` to intersect availability within the bounds of
   `reference/business-hours.md`.
4. Suggest the top few slots; once the user picks, draft the invite from
   `templates/invite.md`.

## Gotchas

- Respect the read rate limit (100/min) when fanning out across calendars.
- Convert to the invitee's timezone using `reference/timezones.md`.
- Suggest, do not book, until the user confirms.

---
name: project-tracker-reporting
description: Roll up project activity into a weekly summary report. Use when the user wants a report, a summary, or a rollup of task status. Runs stored queries; does not create tasks or schedule meetings.
---

# Reporting

Roll up task activity into a summary. Shares nothing with task creation or
scheduling — it runs read-only queries and formats the results.

## Steps

1. Source the shared token: `bash scripts/shared-auth.sh`.
2. Run the stored query: `queries/weekly-rollup.md`.
3. Interpret counts using `reference/metric-definitions.md`.
4. Render the summary with `templates/exec-summary.md`; keep it read-only.

## Gotchas

- Reporting is read-only — never mutate tracker state from here.
- Metric names must match the definitions file exactly.
- Paginate past 100 results (see `reference/api-limits.md`).

---
name: project-tracker-task-creation
description: Create a task in the tracker from a template. Use when the user wants to add a new task, file a request, or open an item. Handles field mapping and validation against the property glossary.
---

# Task creation

Create a single tracker task from a template. This sub-skill owns its own
template and example; nothing here is shared with scheduling or reporting.

## Steps

1. Source the shared token: `bash scripts/shared-auth.sh`.
2. Pick the base template: `templates/task.md` (or `templates/label.md` for
   tracking-only items).
3. Fill the fields, validating `status` against the property glossary and
   tags against `reference/priority-rubric.md`.
4. Submit one create request (see `reference/api-limits.md` for the batch cap).

## Gotchas

- `status` must be one of the closed set; reject anything else.
- Do not send `created_at` — the server sets it.
- One task per request unless the user explicitly asks for a batch.
- Check for duplicates first — see `examples/duplicate-check.md`; surface a
  near-match instead of creating a second task.

# Recursive skill file listings for OpenCode

**A skill is a tree, not a bag of files.** Root `SKILL.md`, plus `reference/`, `scripts/`, `templates/`, `data/` — and, in real practice, **sub-skills**: nested directories that each carry their own `SKILL.md` and cover one distinct capability. Progressive disclosure is the whole design: the agent gets a little metadata up front and reads deeper only when the task calls for it.

That only works if the agent can see the shape of the tree. OpenCode's skill loader samples only the first 10 supporting files in a skill directory; this plugin rewrites the `skill` tool result so the agent sees every file in the directory — recursive, realpaths resolved, capped at 500.

## A skill is a tree

The format says so, and so does practice.

- **The spec defines skills as trees of files.** The [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) allows a skill directory to contain `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`. Anthropic's own write-up calls these "the third level (and beyond) of detail" — [Equipping agents for the real world with agent skills](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills).
- **Practitioners keep building trees-of-skills anyway.** [claude-code#28266](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/28266) is a user with a parent skill and 27 nested sub-skills, filed because the harness only detects the parent. It was closed as a duplicate — of three other requests for the same thing ([#18192](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/18192), [#20805](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/20805), [#10238](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/10238)). This is the pattern being built in the wild while upstream doesn't discover it.
- **Third-party repos use the term.** [alirezarezvani/claude-skills](https://github.com/alirezarezvani/claude-skills) is built as an orchestrator: one root `SKILL.md` routes the agent down into a set of sub-skills.
- **OpenCode states the boundary explicitly.** The [OpenCode skills docs](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/skills/) say: "A directory containing `SKILL.md` is one skill. OpenCode does not search inside it for more skills." It does officially support `SKILL.md` nested in *grouping* directories (`skills/teams/release/SKILL.md`).

**Being honest about it:** the specs describe trees-of-*files*. Nesting whole skills inside skills is a practitioner convention that no major harness fully discovers. This plugin doesn't invent sub-skill discovery — it makes sure the files are visible.

## What the loader shows you

When OpenCode loads a skill, core injects a `<skill_files>` block. It is a **sample, not the directory**. `Skill.prepare()` (`packages/core/src/skill.ts`) does three things, in this order:

1. **Drops every `SKILL.md`** — `.filter((file) => path.basename(file) !== "SKILL.md")`, at any depth. No skill file is ever listed, root or sub-skill.
2. **Sorts** in UTF-16 code-unit order — `.toSorted()`.
3. **Keeps the first ten** — `.slice(0, 10)`.

The result is printed under `Note: file list is sampled.`, which sits *above* the opening tag. The agent gets a flat list of at most 10 paths and nothing else.

A second, related case: when the skill entry isn't the canonical `SKILL.md` (`basename(skill.path) !== "SKILL.md"`), core returns an **empty** `files` list — `<skill_files>` lists nothing at all.

## The listing is mechanical, not meaningful

Neither rule above asks *what this task needs*. The filter erases a sub-skill's entry point, so a branch reads as loose data files rather than as a capability. And the cut at ten is lexicographic: on a skill with more than ten supporting files, what gets dropped is decided by **path ordering**, not importance — a branch whose name sorts late can lose every file, and the agent never learns the branch exists.

It cannot read what it cannot see — and it cannot ask about a capability it has no evidence of.

## The principle: see what it needs, never what it doesn't

The full listing is a **map, not the territory**. Listing ~15 paths costs a few hundred tokens; reading files is what actually costs context. A complete map lets the agent be *more* selective, not less — it navigates precisely to the one branch the task needs instead of blind-reading everything or silently missing a branch.

That's the design goal: the agent sees what it needs and never sees what it doesn't.

## Worked example

[`examples/complex-skill/project-tracker/`](examples/complex-skill/project-tracker/) — 22 files, plus a [README](examples/complex-skill/README.md) alongside it.

```

├── SKILL.md
├── reference/
│   ├── api-limits.md
│   ├── field-mapping.md
│   └── property-glossary.md
├── scripts/
│   ├── new-ticket.sh
│   ├── shared-auth.sh
│   └── status-report.sh
└── skills/
    ├── calendar-scheduling/
    │   ├── SKILL.md
    │   ├── reference/
    │   │   ├── business-hours.md
    │   │   └── timezones.md
    │   ├── scripts/
    │   │   └── find-slots.sh
    │   └── templates/
    │       └── invite.md
    ├── reporting/
    │   ├── SKILL.md
    │   ├── queries/
```

Three **unrelated** sub-skills — `task-creation`, `calendar-scheduling`, `reporting` — unrelated on purpose: two different tasks on this skill need completely different branches. Each carries its own `SKILL.md`; that is what makes it a routable capability.

**Before — what core shows: 10 of 22.** All four `SKILL.md` files are filtered out first, then the ten-file cut applies to the remaining 18 eligible files — and it lands exactly on the `calendar-scheduling` → `reporting` boundary, hiding **two whole branches**: `reporting/` (3 files) and `task-creation/` (5 files). Paths below are relative to the skill root for readability — core actually emits absolute paths:


The agent sees `skills/calendar-scheduling/templates/invite.md` and `scripts/shared-auth.sh` — files from one sub-skill and the root — but nothing that says `reporting/` or `task-creation/` exist at all. Their `SKILL.md` entry points, and every supporting file beneath them, are gone.

Four files reappear, and three of them are sub-skill entry points. Give a skill enough supporting files and the ten-file cut doesn't just strip entry points — it deletes whole branches outright. The plugin restores the four entry points **and** the eight files core dropped, two entire branches (`reporting/`, `task-creation/`) included.

To see it yourself: load the skill in OpenCode with and without the plugin, and diff the `<skill_files>` block.

(The `examples/` directory ships in the repo, not the npm tarball — `package.json` includes only `src/` — so the code blocks above are what npm readers get.)

## What it does

On every completed `skill` tool call, the plugin's `execute.after` hook:

1. Locates the skill directory — `result.metadata.directory` first, then the content's own `Base directory for this skill:` line.
2. Walks it recursively, resolving every path to its realpath (symlinks followed), up to the file cap.
3. Splices a full recursive listing — one `<file>` line per file, sorted — immediately before `</skill_files>` (or `</skill_content>`, or appended).

If the directory can't be resolved, it appends a visible HTML comment saying so and changes nothing else. It never throws and never blocks the tool pipeline.

## Install

Add it to `opencode.json(c)` — a plain string entry in `plugins`. This form works on both OpenCode majors and is the only path for local directories, so it leads:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-recursive-skills"]
}
```

Or install with the CLI's `add` subcommand:

```bash
opencode plugin add opencode-recursive-skills
```

> **Historical (v1):** OpenCode v1 used the bare-positional form `opencode plugin <package>`. That form is v1-only — on v2 it exits 1. Use `plugin add` or the config array above.

With options:

```jsonc
{
  "plugins": [
    {
      "package": "opencode-recursive-skills",
      "options": {
        "maxFiles": 300,
        "debug": false
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

> **Local development:** for a local checkout, prefer a `~/…` (home-relative) entry in `plugins`. On v2.1.2 an absolute-path or relative entry pointing at this package was silently ignored (its entrypoint is declared only via `package.json` `exports`, with no root-level `index.ts`), while the `~/…` form loaded fine. Confirm with `--print-logs`: look for `msg="loading plugin"` whose `id=` is your configured target.

## Verify it's working

Load any skill and look for the plugin's marker in the `skill` tool result, immediately before the closing tag:

```
<!-- recursive-skills: recursive list (N files) -->
```

`N` is the number of files the walk found (with `(capped at …)` appended if it hit the cap). If the directory couldn't be resolved, you'll instead see `recursive file list unavailable (skill directory could not be resolved)`.

For a step-by-step trace, set `RECURSIVE_SKILLS_DEBUG=1` (or `"debug": true` in options) and watch stderr for `[recursive-skills]` lines.

## The trade-off

The ten-file cap is deliberate — core prints `Note: file list is sampled.` and, for most skills, ten supporting files are enough. This plugin intentionally spends some context for completeness: on a large skill the spliced block adds many `<file>` lines to the tool result, and each line rides along on later turns that still carry that result.

- **Bound it** — set `maxFiles` (or `RECURSIVE_SKILLS_MAX_FILES`) low; the walk stops at the cap and the marker notes `(capped at N)`.
- **Opt out** — remove the plugin from `plugins` to restore core's sampled behavior. There is no per-skill toggle.

## Compatibility

- Requires **OpenCode V2**. Tested against **v2.1.2**.
- Depends on the `execute.after` hook payload shape — `event.tool`, `event.status`, and `event.result.content` as a string or an array of `{type:"text"}` parts containing `<skill_content`. v2.1.2 delivers the **array** form at runtime (a string branch is kept as fallback).
- If a future OpenCode changes that payload shape, or the skill directory can't be resolved, the hook **no-ops** — no error, no crash; the skill just loads unsampled.

## Options

| Option | Env var | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `maxFiles` | `RECURSIVE_SKILLS_MAX_FILES` | `500` | Safety cap on listed files |
| `debug` | `RECURSIVE_SKILLS_DEBUG=1` | `false` | Opt-in debug logging (silent by default) |

Options beat env vars beat the default.

## How it works

Registers `ctx.tool.hook("execute.after", ...)` via `Plugin.define` from `@opencode/plugin`. Only the `skill` tool is touched (`event.tool !== "skill"` returns early), and only completed results. Core re-reads `result.content` after hooks resolve, so the rewrite reaches the model. The content arrives as an **array** of `{type:"text"}` parts; the plugin finds the part containing `<skill_content`, rewrites that part's `text`, and returns a new result — a string-content branch is kept as a fallback.

## Limitations

- **Lists, doesn't promote** — nested `SKILL.md` files become visible as files; the harness still loads only the top-level skill.
- **Lists dotfiles** — the walk doesn't filter leading dots, matching core's own `dot: true` scan.
- **No general ignore-glob filtering** — only the hardcoded `SKIP_DIRS` set (`node_modules`, `.git`) is excluded from the walk; any other large tree counts against `maxFiles`.
- **500-file cap** — a ceiling, not a sample. Raise or lower it via `maxFiles`.

## Safety notes

- **Bounded** — the walk stops at `maxFiles`, which also guards symlink loops and pathological trees.
- **Fail-silent** — an unresolvable directory, a broken symlink, a vanished file, or any hook error is swallowed; the skill still loads. The unresolvable-directory case leaves a visible HTML comment rather than failing.
- **No network** — the plugin only reads the local filesystem.

# Example: a skill tree that outgrows the 10-file cap

This example shows why a real skill is a **tree, not a flat list of 10 files**:
load `project-tracker/` in OpenCode with and without this plugin and compare the
`<skill_files>` block, and you will see the built-in loader silently hide whole
sub-skill branches while the plugin lists every path.

## The real mechanism (corrected)

An earlier version of this example claimed core sorts *all* files and slices
the first 10 — as if `SKILL.md` files counted. They don't. Verified against the
bundled `Skill.prepare` in the OpenCode v2.1.2 release binary, the file sample
is built as:

```
scan("**/*")                                // every file under the skill dir
  .filter((file) => basename(file) !== "SKILL.md")   // ← SKILL.md removed FIRST
  .toSorted()                               // UTF-16 code-unit order
  .slice(0, 10)                             // then the cap
```

So the 10-file cap counts only a skill's **supporting files** (reference,
templates, scripts, examples, queries). Every `SKILL.md` — including the one
being loaded — is filtered out before sorting and never appears in the sample
at all. A skill with 4 `SKILL.md` files and 9 supporting files never hits the
cap; a skill with more than 10 supporting files does.

## What to notice

`project-tracker/` has three unrelated sub-skills — `task-creation`,
`calendar-scheduling`, and `reporting`. It has **18 supporting files**, so the
cap engages: core shows the first **10** and hides **8**. The sort is
alphabetical, and `task-creation` and `reporting` both come after
`calendar-scheduling`, so **the cut lands exactly at a sub-skill boundary and
the entire supporting file set of two branches disappears**:

- `sub-skills/task-creation/` — all 5 of its supporting files hidden
- `sub-skills/reporting/` — all 3 of its supporting files hidden

The agent sees the root's shared files and all of `calendar-scheduling`, then
the list simply stops. A map that omits whole branches is worse than no map,
because the agent cannot navigate to what it cannot see.

## Command shape (do not run — this is the shape)

Load the skill both ways and diff the `<skill_files>` block:

```
# without the plugin (core's 10-file sample)
<skill name="project-tracker" />          # then read the <skill_files> block

# with opencode-recursive-skills enabled
<skill name="project-tracker" />          # <skill_files> now lists all 22 paths
```

Compare: the plugin's block contains every path in the tree — all 22 files,
including the four `SKILL.md` files that core filtered out; core's block stops
at 10 supporting files and never mentions `task-creation/` or `reporting/`.

## The honest first-10 computation

**How this was produced (stated so it can be checked):** the sorted list below
is **computed, not captured** — it was produced by replaying the exact pipeline
quoted above against the real files in `project-tracker/` (recursive file
walk, filter out every `SKILL.md`, default `toSorted()`, `slice(0, 10)`).
Paths are shown skill-relative; core prefixes them with the absolute skill
directory, which does not change the order. A live capture was not taken
because invoking the skill tool requires a model run against a registered
skill; the computation mirrors the v2.1.2 binary's bundled source line for
line. All 18 supporting files, in the exact order core sorts them:

```
 1. reference/api-limits.md                                            (shown)
 2. reference/field-mapping.md                                         (shown)
 3. reference/property-glossary.md                                     (shown)
 4. scripts/new-ticket.sh                                              (shown)
 5. scripts/shared-auth.sh                                             (shown)
 6. scripts/status-report.sh                                           (shown)
 7. sub-skills/calendar-scheduling/reference/business-hours.md         (shown)
 8. sub-skills/calendar-scheduling/reference/timezones.md              (shown)
 9. sub-skills/calendar-scheduling/scripts/find-slots.sh               (shown)
10. sub-skills/calendar-scheduling/templates/invite.md                 (shown)
--- core's slice(0, 10) ends here ---
11. sub-skills/reporting/queries/weekly-rollup.md                      (hidden)
12. sub-skills/reporting/reference/metric-definitions.md               (hidden)
13. sub-skills/reporting/templates/exec-summary.md                     (hidden)
14. sub-skills/task-creation/examples/completed-task.md                (hidden)
15. sub-skills/task-creation/examples/duplicate-check.md               (hidden)
16. sub-skills/task-creation/reference/priority-rubric.md              (hidden)
17. sub-skills/task-creation/templates/label.md                        (hidden)
18. sub-skills/task-creation/templates/task.md                         (hidden)
```

**Core shows files 1–10. The cap hides files 11–18** — the complete supporting
file set of the `task-creation/` branch *and* of the `reporting/` branch. The
`SKILL.md` files (root plus one per sub-skill, 4 total) are not in this list at
all: they were filtered before the sort, so they neither consume slots nor
rescue their branches.

Note on depth: the hidden set includes the deepest files in the tree
(`task-creation/templates/task.md`, `reporting/queries/weekly-rollup.md`), but
depth is not what decides the cut — alphabetical order is. A deeper file placed
early alphabetically (e.g. `calendar-scheduling/templates/invite.md`, position
10) is shown, while shallower files placed late (`reporting/reference/…`,
position 12) are hidden.

## File count

22 files total under `project-tracker/` — 4 `SKILL.md` + 18 supporting files
(23 with this README). 18 > 10, so the cap bites: 10 shown, 8 hidden.

# API limits

Shared rate limits for the tracker API. Check before batching writes.

- Read requests: 100 / minute per session token.
- Write requests: 25 / minute per session token.
- Batch create: max 20 items per request.
- Search / query: max 100 results per page; paginate past that.

A `429` means back off and retry with exponential delay. Do not loop tightly.

# Field mapping

Where each tracker field comes from when building a request body.

- `title` — from the user's ask, condensed to one line.
- `status` — always starts at `todo`; only the task-creation flow advances it later.
- `assignee` — the named owner; leave empty rather than guessing.
- `due_date` — ISO date or empty; never an approximate phrase like "next week".
- `tags` — lowercase strings; reuse existing tags before inventing new ones.

Unknown fields are rejected, not passed through. If a requested field is not
in this list or in the property glossary, ask instead of forwarding it.

# Property glossary

Field names used across tracker objects.

- `title` — short human label.
- `status` — one of `todo`, `in_progress`, `blocked`, `done`.
- `assignee` — the person responsible.
- `due_date` — ISO date; may be empty.
- `tags` — free-form list of strings.
- `created_at` — set by the server; never sent by the client.

Values for `status` are closed — reject anything outside the list above.

# Business hours

Working-day bounds used when intersecting availability. Slots outside these
bounds are not offered even if a calendar is technically free.

- Weekdays only; weekends are offered only on explicit request.
- Working day: 09:00–17:00 in the host's local time.
- Minimum slot: 15 minutes; default duration: 30 minutes.
- Leave a 15-minute buffer at the start of the working day.

Convert the bounds into the host's timezone before intersecting; see
`timezones.md` for IANA labels.

# Timezones

Common timezone labels for converting suggested slots to an invitee's local
time. Pick the IANA name, never an abbreviation like "CST" (ambiguous).

- `America/New_York`
- `America/Chicago`
- `America/Denver`
- `America/Los_Angeles`
- `Europe/London`

Always present a suggested slot in both the host and invitee timezones.

# Invite template

title: ""
start: "" # ISO datetime in the host timezone
duration_min: 30
location: ""

# Fill every field before suggesting. Never send an invite until the user
# confirms a slot. Present the start time in both the host and invitee
# timezones (see reference/timezones.md).

# Weekly rollup query

Read-only query that groups tasks by status for the past 7 days.

    FROM tasks
    WHERE updated_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
    GROUP BY status

Returns one row per status value with a count. Order by status. Do not add
write clauses — this query must stay read-only.

# Metric definitions

Names used in reporting output. Match these exactly; do not invent synonyms.

- `open_count` — tasks with status `todo` or `in_progress`.
- `blocked_count` — tasks with status `blocked`.
- `done_count` — tasks with status `done`.
- `throughput` — tasks moved to `done` within the window.

Each metric maps to exactly one row from the rollup query.

# Example: duplicate check before create

Search for an existing match on `title` before creating a task. Two records
that would be considered the same task:

title: "File expense report"
title: "File expense report" # same title, same assignee -> duplicate

title: "File expense report"
title: "File Q4 expense report" # different scope -> not a duplicate

If a close match exists, surface it to the user instead of creating a second
task. Do not merge or edit existing tasks from this sub-skill.

# Priority rubric

How to pick tags that convey urgency when the user does not specify one.

- `p1` — blocks someone else's work right now.
- `p2` — due within the current week.
- `p3` — everything else with a due date.
- no priority tag — no due date; add one only if asked.

Priority is expressed through `tags`, not a separate field. Never guess a
due date just to justify a priority tag.
